_[![](data:image/png;base64,)](http://crossmark.crossref.org/dialog/?doi=10.1016/j.carbpol.2021.118735&domain=pdf)_Adsorption properties of heavy metals and antibiotics by chitosan from larvae and adult _Trypoxylus dichotomus_

A R T I C L E I N F O

_Keywords:_

Composite contaminants Multi-step protein purification Hydrothermal deacetylation Adsorbent

A B S T R A C T

Chitosan was prepared by hydrothermal deacetylation from multi-step protein purification chitin based on _Trypoxylus dichotomus_, for treating heavy metals and antibiotics. Chitosan with higher deacetylation degree and lower molecular weight were synthesized. The adult chitosan was composed of nanofibers arranged more evenly,

showing higher yield, thermal stabilities and antimicrobial properties. The adsorption capacities of Cu2+ and Fe3+ were 462 and 270 mg/g, lower than 934 mg/g of Pb2+. Levofloxacin and tetracycline hydrochloride

adsorption capacity were 26 and 22 mg/g, lower than 67 mg/g of sulfamethoxazole. In addition, compared with single pollutants, the adsorption of sulfamethoxazole and Pb2+ can increase by 6% and 5% when they act as composite contaminants. The adsorption procedure can be well described by pseudo-second-order kinetics and

Langmuir isothermal model, indicating it a homogeneous monolayer chemisorption. Therefore, the _Trypoxylus dichotomus_ source chitosan prepared by hydrothermal deacetylation has potential applications in the adsorption of complex pollutants.

# Introduction

Due to the continuous rise of industrial level, water resource con-sumption is huge, and water pollution caused by complex pollutants is increasingly serious. Some heavy metal ions are toxic to the human body. For example, plumbum may cause serious damage to the axial nervous system, kidney and liver ([Fu & Wang, 2011](#_bookmark46)). In addition, an-tibiotics usually contain hydroxyl, carboxyl, amine and other functional groups, which may form a series of complexes with different valence states when coexisting with heavy metal ions, thus further changing their toxicity ([Pinheiro, Rosa Albano, Alves, Kaufmann, & da Silva,](#_bookmark70) [2013](#_bookmark70)). It is well known that chitosan has good reactivity and chelating ability, which is very suitable for simultaneous adsorption of various pollutants in water ([Ahmed, Hameed, & Hummadi, 2020](#_bookmark29); [Jia et al.,](#_bookmark53) [2016](#_bookmark53); [Usman et al., 2021](#_bookmark85); [Wang & Zhuang, 2017](#_bookmark86)). However, the prac-tical application of composite pollutant adsorption has high cost, low efficiency and complex process, so new chitosan materials are urgently needed to meet the requirements of adsorbent ([Pap et al., 2020](#_bookmark68)).

Chitosan is obtained by deacetylation of chitin, which is the only natural alkaline polysaccharide discovered so far ([Chen et al., 2018](#_bookmark37)). However, chitin resources now available have some challenges, including insufficient supplies, seasonal availability, and environmental pollution ([Mohan et al., 2020](#_bookmark65)). Recently, there have been a great deal of studies on insects as the source of chitin, because there are more ad-vantages to extracting chitin and chitosan from insects, such as repro-ductive rate ([Ma, Xin, & Tan, 2015](#_bookmark64)), moderate conditions ([Zhao, Park, &](#_bookmark95) [Muzzarelli, 2010](#_bookmark95)) and ability to convert catastrophic species into commercialization ([Purkayastha & Sarkar, 2020](#_bookmark71)), over existing sources in terms of extraction methods, chemical consumption and yield ([Bat-tampara et al., 2020](#_bookmark32); [Kaya, Sofi, Sargin and Mujtaba, 2016](#_bookmark59); [Saenz-Mendoza et al., 2020](#_bookmark75)). During the growth of the same insect, the content of chitin changes to some extent, and the larval stage of the unicorns takes up two-thirds of its one-year life span, so taking into account of time and economic costs, it is indispensable to study the chitin at different growth stages ([Kaya, Sofi, Sargin, & Mujtaba, 2016](#_bookmark59); [Mohan](#_bookmark65) [et al., 2020](#_bookmark65); [Zhang et al., 2018](#_bookmark92); [Zhang, Zaslavski, Vasilyev, Boas, &](#_bookmark93)

Coleoptera is the largest biota and the most commonly eaten insect globally ([Belluco et al., 2013](#_bookmark33)). Chitin from _Polyphylla Fullo_ and _Holo-trichia Parallela_ of Coleoptera has been shown to be a reliable chitin substitute source ([Kabalak, Aracago¨k, & Torun, 2020](#_bookmark55); [Liu et al., 2012](#_bookmark62)). As a member of Coleoptera, _T. dichotomus_ feeds on humus or wood chips. Due to its convenient feeding and strong breeding potential ([Yang et al.,](#_bookmark88) [2021](#_bookmark88)), it has been raised as food for a long time in Asia, mainly in Korea, Japan, China and Thailand ([Lee et al., 2021](#_bookmark61)). The male _T. dichotomus_ has a single horn with a forked tip and is kept as a pet because of this unique appearance. Recently, due to its scavenging nature, _T. dichotomus_ has been widely applied to the disposal of waste such as fungus chaff, but the bodies of _T. dichotomus_ are usually left to decay naturally without treatment methods. The research on _T. dichotomus_ is commonly found in the populations and their wings ([Truong et al., 2012](#_bookmark84); [Yang et al., 2020](#_bookmark87)). Besides, the use of _T. dichotomus_ as a source of chitin and chitosan has not been reported.

The deacetylation process of the conversion of chitin to chitosan has a great influence on the properties of chitosan ([Park, Je, & Kim, 2004](#_bookmark69); [Sayari et al., 2016](#_bookmark77)). However, the traditional heating method of deacetylation in water bath or oil bath has strict requirements on re-action conditions such as alkali concentration, temperature and time ([Domard & Rinaudo, 1983](#_bookmark43)). After the reaction, it is difficult to collect the waste lye, and the equipment requires hot reaction and corrosion of heat-resistant alkali. The hydrothermal method in material preparation and chemical treatment is completed in a closed uniform system, in which the chemicals can be safely recycled. Additionally, it is an envi-ronmentally friendly technology, which takes place under moderate heating conditions and autogenous pressure and has excellent control-lability in the morphology, size and chemical composition of the re-actants, and the reaction efficiency can be greatly improved ([Chagas,](#_bookmark36) [Crispim, Pinto, San Gil, & Mota, 2020](#_bookmark36)). The process is simple, with low production costs, and does not make use of organic solvents, catalysts, or surfactants, and have been proven to be an excellent way to produce porous materials with strong adsorption effect ([Laginhas, Nabais, &](#_bookmark60) [Titirici, 2016](#_bookmark60)). In this study, chitosan from _T. dichotomus_ larvae and adults was prepared by hydrothermal deacetylation for the first time after the multi-step protein purification of chitin. Furthermore, their morphology, thermal stability, antimicrobial activity and adsorption capacity. The aim was to prepare a chitosan polymer from _Trypoxylus dichotomus_ and to study its use in removing heavy metals and antibiotics from aqueous solutions.

Hypotheses:

The chitosan from _Trypoxylus dichotomus_ adults has the synergistic adsorption abilities of heavy metals and antibiotics at a certain concentration.

# Experimental

- 1.  _Materials_

In September 2020, _T. dichotomus_ adults and larvae that died natu-rally within 3 days were obtained from Jilin Province Technology Research Center of Biological Control Engineering ([Fig. 1](#_bookmark6)(a, b, c)). They

were collected from Changbai Mountain (127◦42′55′′ E to 128◦16′48′′ E, 41◦41′49′′ N to 42◦51′18′′ N) (see Fig. S1). The adults originally stored at

—80 ◦C and the larvae immersed in 70% ethanol solution were washed with distilled water, removed internal organs, and cut into 5 mm × 20 mm pieces with surgical scissors, and dried at 65 ◦C to constant weight. Standard chitin, standard chitosan and commercial chitosan (degree of

deacetylation from 75 to 85%, viscosity-based molecular weight of 50,000–190,000 Da) was purchased from Sigma-Aldrich Chemical Co. (Shanghai, China) and used to compare the adsorption performance.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Fig. 1.** Camera pictures of _T. dichotomus_. a) larvae, b) male adult, c) fe-male adult.

- 1.  _Chitin extraction_

The extraction procedure of chitin was based on Chen et al. and improved on this basis ([Chen et al., 2021](#_bookmark38); [Chen, Tang, Wang, & Zhang,](#_bookmark40) [2021](#_bookmark40)). Using n-hexane as solvent, the raw materials of larvae and adults

were defatted in 80 ◦C water bath for 3 h by soxhlet extraction. The obtained powder was dried at 65 ◦C for 8 h. Degreased powder was deproteinized by 4 rounds of hot alkali bath. In the first round, the

powder (1 g) was mixed with 30 mL of 0.5 M NaOH solution. Heat the mixture, stirring at 95 ◦C and 500 rpm for 20 min. The residual powder was separated by centrifugation at 4000 rpm for 20 s and then rinsed

with distilled water to neutral. In the second round, the residual powder after the first round was mixed with NaOH solution again at the same temperature and stirring speed. The volume, NaOH concentration and reaction time were changed to 5 mL, 4 M and 80 min, respectively. The residual powder is then separated and rinsed as described above. The conditions for the third and fourth rounds were the same as for the second, except that the reaction time was changed to 150 min and 30 min respectively. After deproteinization, the remaining powder was

dried in an oven at 105 ◦C for 10 h. Continue with each step until ab-

sorption of the supernatant ceases to increase at 280 nm (referring to bull serum albumin). The deproteinized powder was demineralized by 5 mL 0.5 M HCl for 1 h at 60 ◦C and 500 rpm. The residual powder is then

separated, washed and dried as described above. The residual powder

was _T. dichotomus_ larvae and adult chitin after being bleached with 5 mL 10% H2O2 at 80 ◦C and 500 rpm for 3 h, then separated, rinsed and dried at 80 ◦C for 24 h.

- 1.  _Hydrothermal deacetylation process_

2 g of the decolorization product was mixed with 60 mL NaOH so-lution (50 wt%) and placed in a polytetrafluoroethylene reaction still with a volume of 100 mL. The hydrothermal conditions for experimental group are set under temperature at 100, 125,150 and 175 ◦C for 6.0 h to explore the optimal hydrothermal temperature. Besides, at the optimal

temperature above, 6 h was shortened to 4.5 h, 3 h and 1.5 h, respec-tively, to explore the optimal hydrothermal time (see Table S1 for the conditions). Then the residual powder was separated by centrifugation

at 4000 rpm for 20 s, rinse with deionized water to neutrality (the pH value to 7.0) and dry at 105 ◦C for 8 h to obtain adult and larvae chi-tosan. Since the extraction of chitin and chitosan from _T. dichotomus_ has

never been reported before, the conventional alkaline heating method was processed as a control. The deacetylation process was carried out with a polytetrafluoroethylene 100 mL beaker in a sand bath, temper-ature and time adjusted according to the above methods, and the rest of

the conditions remain the same (see Table S1).

- 1.  _Antimicrobial activity_

The disc diffusion method was used to determine the antimicrobial activity of chitin and chitosan from _T. dichotomus_ adults and larvae. The 20 mg product was pressed into a 6 mm diameter disc, and either the front or back sides of the material were irradiated with ultraviolet light for 30 min. The disc diffusion method was used to determine the anti-microbial activity against _Staphylococcus aureus_, _Bacillus subtilis_, _Salmo-nella para-typhi B_ (gram-positive bacterium), _Escherichia coli_, _Pseudomonas aeruginosa_ (gram-negative bacterium) and _Candida albicans_

(fungi). Suspend the microorganisms in LB or PB liquid medium at 37 ◦C for 24 h, and adjust the suspension to 4.8 × 107 cfu/mL (by optical

density). In the disc diffusion method, the disks were placed on the agar medium inoculated with 300 μL of microbial suspensions. Each experi-ment was repeated three times. After incubation at 37 ◦C for 24 h, the

circles of inhibition formed around the sample were photographed and measured.

- 1.  _Statistical analysis_

All quantitative data are expressed as mean ± standard deviation. A method of analysis of variance was performed using the STATISTICA software. One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) and a p-test were used

to identify the significance of any effects of single and composite contaminant adsorption properties of the chitosan prepared by hydro-thermal deacetylation. The difference between the samples was evalu-ated by the Tukey test (α = 0.05).

- 1.  _Component characteristics_

The contribution of temperature and time to DD and Mv is shown. It can be seen from [Fig. 2](#_bookmark19) (a) that hydrothermal temperature has a positive effect on the deacetylation degree of chitosan of larvae and adults. When the temperature reached 150 ◦C, the deacetylation degree of larvae and

adults reached 85% and 91%, respectively, and remained stable. The

hydrothermal temperature had a negative effect on the chitosan Mv of larvae and adults. At 150 ◦C, the molecular weight of chitosan larvae and adults decreased by 45% and 46%, respectively, compared with that of chitin. However, after 150 ◦C, the effect of temperature on DD and Mv is no longer obvious. This is because NaOH will degrade the glycosidic

bonds in the chitin chain under heating conditions, turning it into small fragments or single sugar molecules, and realizing deacetylation. Therefore, the DD of both larvae and adult chitosan increases and the Mv decreases during the whole hydrothermal process. When the tempera-ture increases, the speed of the NaOH molecule movement increases, which is conducive to the reaction. Therefore, comprehensively

considering economic benefits and safety, 150 ◦C is selected as the

temperature of hydrothermal treatment. Then, the time conditions of the hydrothermal were explored at the same treatment temperature of

150 ◦C in [Fig. 2](#_bookmark19) (b). With the progress of the reaction, the DD of chitosan in larvae and adults showed an upward trend, and reached 85% and 92%

at 4.5 h. Meanwhile, the Mv showed a downward trend, and reached 147 and 97 kDa at 4.5 h. After that, time had no significant effect on DD and Mv of chitosan. For the deacetylation of chitosan treated by heating and stirring in the same solution environment (see Fig. S2), 83% and 80%

deacetylation degrees of adult and larvae chitosan were obtained at 175 ◦C for 24 h, and the molecular weight of that decreased by 23% and 20%. Therefore, based on reaction efficiency and economic benefits, the

chitosan products after hydrothermal treatment at 150 ◦C for 4.5 h were used for further research, and are referred to as larvae and adult chitosan for short.

The elemental content of _T. dichotomus_, _T. dichotomus_ chitin and chitosan was determined by elemental analysis. As shown in [Table 1](#_bookmark20), since the protein content of _T. dichotomus_ is much higher than that of chitin and chitosan, the protein content of _T. dichotomus_ can be calcu-lated by the content of N element to be 79.13% for adult and 79.64% for larvae. The content of N element in chitosan and chitin products decreased to 1/2 or less than that of the original materials after multi-step protein removal. The N% of larval chitosan is 6.639%, and its low nitrogen content may be related to a slightly higher degree of mineral-ization ([Sajomsang & Gonil, 2010](#_bookmark76)), however, the N% of adult chitosan is 6.703%, which is closer to the theoretical N% of fully deacetylated chitosan ([Liu et al., 2012](#_bookmark62)). The sulfur content of chitosan products is lower than that of _T. dichotomus_ and commercial chitosan, and the sulfur content of adult chitosan is zero. Owing that sulfur content is closely related to protein content, protein removal is realized in the multi-step deproteinization process and the subsequent hydrothermal deacetyla-tion process, which is an alternative to the conventional protein removal method. In addition, the elemental composition of larval chitosan, adult chitosan and commercial chitosan is similar.

The component characteristics of chitin and chitosan from larvae and

adult _T. dichotomus_ are shown in [Table 1](#_bookmark20). According to calculations, the chitin and chitosan yields of larvae are lower than those of adults. The results of the viscosity test showed that the average molecular weight of adult chitin and chitosan was 170 kDa and 97 kDa, lower than that of larvae (257 kDa and 147 kDa) and lower than chitosan of shrimp and crab shells (280 kDa and 140 kDa) ([Zhang, Xi, Chen, & Bai, 2020](#_bookmark91)). By consulting important literature, _T. dichotomus_ has the advantage of being the raw material of chitin compared to other _Coleoptera_ (the yield of Colorado Potato Beetle (_Leptinotarsa decemlineata_) was 7% of the larval and 20% of the adult ([Kaya et al., 2014](#_bookmark58)). The yield of _Mealworm Beetle_ was 4.6% of larval and 8.4% of adult, while that of _Rhinoceros Beetle_ was 10.5% of larval and 14.2% of adult ([Shin, Kim, & Shin, 2019](#_bookmark79)). The DA values of adult and larvae chitin are relatively close, but the DD value of adult chitosan is significantly higher than that of larvae, which may be due to different deacetylation transitions caused by different properties of chitin. In addition, it was found during the analysis that the chitosan of both adults and larvae can be completely dissolved in 1% acetic acid at room temperature. According to [Table 2](#_bookmark21), compared with that of shrimps, crabs and other _Coleoptera i_nsects, the chitosan yields of adults and larvae of _T. Dichotomus_ prepared through hydrothermal method (12.0% and 11.0%) were close to those of shrimps and crabs for commercial sources and had higher degree of deacetylation (92% and 85%).

- 1.  _Apparent morphology_

To prove that hydrothermal chitosan deacetylation does not affect the effect of decolorization in the multi-step deproteinization process. Fig. S3 shows the apparent morphology of the product _T. dichotomus_ chitin and chitosan. The chitin prepared by the multi-step protein pu-rification step has a white flaky structure, while the chitosan prepared by hydrothermal deacetylation treatment presents a slightly darker

beige, and the chitosan products of adults are lighter in color than those of larvae, which is closer to the color of commercially available high-purity chitosan ([Shin et al., 2019](#_bookmark79).

- 1.  _FTIR analysis_

The chemical functional groups of chitin and chitosan were analyzed by FT-IR. As shown in [Fig. 2](#_bookmark19) (c), the adult and the larvae chitin show

α-chitin characteristic peaks at 1664, 1619, and 1561 cm—1, corre-sponding to the stretching vibration peaks of the C–O bond of the amide

I band, the bending of the N–H bond and the stretching vibration peak of the C–N bond of the amide II band ([Qin, Jia, Liu, Kong, & Wang,](#_bookmark72) [2019](#_bookmark72); [Srinivasan, Kanayairam, & Ravichandran, 2018](#_bookmark80)). For the chitosan product, the corresponding peak at 1561 cm—1 was weak due to the high

deacetylation degree. In addition, O–H absorption and N–H stretching

band appear near 3500 and 3264 cm—1. We can also see that the char-acteristic peaks of C–O in the chitosan amide I band and the NH2 in the amide II band are in the larvae (1658 and 1600 cm—1) and adult chitosan (1674 and 1590 cm—1). In addition, the shoulder peaks at 895 and 1160 cm—1 are also related to the structure of chitosan. Chitin and chitosan of both larvae and adults showed similar FTIR peaks while the intensities

were different, indicating that the major components of chitin did not change significantly with the growth of _T. dichotomus_ ([Luo et al., 2019](#_bookmark63)). Besides, the FTIR spectrometric measurement is consistent with the DD

% value of the chitosan measured by the methyl orange-aniline blue titration method ([Zhang, Xu, et al., 2018](#_bookmark92); [Zhang, Zaslavski, et al., 2018](#_bookmark93)).

- 1.  _XRD analysis_

The product chitin and chitosan were analyzed by X-ray diffraction ([Fig. 2](#_bookmark19) d–g) to study the crystal structure and estimate the crystallinity. The crystallization characteristic peaks of larvae and the adult chitin at 9.3◦, 19.3◦ and 23.4◦ coincided with the characteristic peaks of α- chitin

([Hong et al., 2019](#_bookmark49)). At 26.6◦, the peak intensity of larvae chitin is

significantly higher than that of adult chitin, which indicates that larvae chitin has a wider amorphous structure, that is, the amorphous domains with structural defects. The peaks of adult and larvae chitosan are both in the amorphous domains at 11.4◦ and 20.2◦, but the peak of adult

chitosan is lower, which corresponds to the high crystalline index of

adult chitosan ([Table 1](#_bookmark20)) ([Gbenebor, Adeosun, Lawal, Jun, & Olaleye,](#_bookmark47) [2017](#_bookmark47)) and slightly shifts to a higher diffraction angle and showed semi-crystalline chitosan (compared to that of crab chitosan at 10.3◦ and

19.2◦) ([Purkayastha & Sarkar, 2020](#_bookmark71)). In combination with the CrI values

shown in [Table 1](#_bookmark20) and reported in the literature, compared with the adult _Hermetia illucens_ with irregular surface and high CrI (87.92%), the chi-tosan with porous surface morphology obtained in this study have lower CrI (83.2% and 83.6%), which may be related to the fact that the multi-step deproteinization process increases the amorphous properties and reduces the insect protein microcrystallinity ([Caligiani et al., 2018](#_bookmark35)).

Besides, the maximum degradation temperatures of them are 361 ◦C and 335 ◦C. For chitosan, the water evaporation stage of the larvae and adults accounted for only 1%, while 76% of the mass

loss of the adult and 67% of the larvae correspond to the chitosan degradation. The maximum degradation temperature of adults and larvae is 413 ◦C and 405 ◦C, respectively. For the commercial chitosan

source of shrimp and crab shells, three stages of heat loss (below 100 ◦C,

about 250 ◦C, and above 350 ◦C) were demonstrated, and the decom-position reached complete at about 500 ◦C (mass loss ranged from 57%

to 96%) ([Andrade, Ladchumananandasivam, Rocha, Belarmino, &](#_bookmark30) [Galv˜ao, 2012](#_bookmark30)). Combined with the results of the decomposition of the above products at higher temperatures, the chitosan from _T. dichotomus_ adult had a more stable unit composition, and the chitosan degradation stage may be related to its crystallinity. In addition, DSC confirmed that the chitosan obtained was different from chitin, and had typical poly-saccharide behavior, including dehydration and degradation stages ([Synytsya et al., 2009](#_bookmark82)).

- 1.  _13C NMR analysis_

[Fig. 2](#_bookmark19) (j–l) shows the 13C NMR of the product larval chitosan, adult chitosan and standard chitosan to determine the properties and purity of the chitosan. According to the spectral structure, the C3 and C5 peaks of larval and adult chitosan almost overlapped each other and showed a single peak at _δ_ 75.2 ppm and _δ_ 75.3 ppm, and the C4 showed a weak signal peak splitting. The signals of C-5, C-3, C-6 and C-2 do not show the same behavior as observed in other spectra, which is similar to the chitosan prepared from shrimp residues as reported ([Borja-Urzola et al.,](#_bookmark34) [2020](#_bookmark34)). In addition, the three chitosan had a low CH3 peak (_δ_ 19.8 ppm), which was consistent with the results of FT-IR analysis, corresponding to the high degree of deacetylation of the products. Importantly, according to [Figs. 2](#_bookmark19) (c), (h-i), (l) and S5, the peak range of _T. dichotomus_ chitin and chitosan prepared was similar to that of the standard substance, but

there was only a slight numerical difference, which might be related to the source of materials and deacetylation process. It was confirmed that the physical and chemical properties of _T. dichotomus_ chitin and chitosan were very close to that of the standards.

- 1.  _SEM_

According to the SEM ([Fig. 3](#_bookmark22) a–d), it has been observed that the chitin and chitosan from _T. dichotomus_ larvae and adults have a unique dimensional fibrous mesh pore structure ([Zhu, Gu, Hong, & Lian, 2017](#_bookmark96)). After the hydrothermal deacetylation step, the transition from porous sheet to fiber network is more obvious. The surface of larvae chitin is rough, the pore size distribution is quite different, and the diameter distribution of the corresponding deacetylated chitosan fiber is also large, which may be caused by the lack of uniform distribution of exoskeleton to protect the internal structure before metamorphosis development ([Kaya, Sofi, et al., 2016](#_bookmark59)). Adult chitosan fibers are more uniform than larvae, showing a three-dimensional porous surface morphology, which have great potential in practical applications such as adsorption materials and tissue engineering. The porous structure is similar to that obtained from lobster shells by using a mixture of choline chloride, but the fibrous bundles are more evenly arranged ([Hong, Yuan,](#_bookmark50) [Yang, Zhu, & Lian, 2018](#_bookmark50); [Zhu et al., 2017](#_bookmark96)). It is worth mentioning that commercial chitosan is agglomerated and does not have the fibrous mesh pore structure (see Fig. S4).

- 1.  _Antimicrobial activity_

The antimicrobial activity of chitin and chitosan from adults and larvae was studied ([Abral et al., 2020](#_bookmark28)). [Fig. 4](#_bookmark23) (A-B) and [Table 3](#_bookmark24) show the results of disc diffusion, the chitin from _T. dichotomus_ larvae and adults have only a minimal inhibitory effect on microorganisms (<130%). Obviously, the diameters of the antimicrobial inhibition zones of the two

were both greater than 6 mm, which demonstrated the antimicrobial activity of _T. dichotomus_ chitosans, among which the inhibitory effect of

bacteria), the cell wall of _S. aureus_ (gram-positive bacteria) not only has acidic environment, but also has no lipid and protein outside the cell wall of gram-positive bacteria, which is favorable for chitosan to exert its inhibitory effect. The possible mechanism of the phenomenon is due to the interaction between positively charged chitosan chain and negatively charged microbial cell membranes, which leads to the destruction of bacterial cell, which is consistent with commercial chi-tosan ([Chien, Yen, & Mau, 2016](#_bookmark41)). It is interesting that many highly effective antibacterial materials also show certain differences in their inhibitory effects on gram-negative and gram-positive bacteria, and the mechanism is also related to the differences in their cell structures ([Pandey & Ramontja, 2016](#_bookmark67)). The inhibitory effect on _C. albicans_ is also due to this polycationic property of chitosan, which reacts with nega-tively charged components of the cell membrane, which results in cell membrane destruction and thus prevents adhesion to both biotic and abiotic surfaces ([Rubini, Vedha Hari, & Nithyanand, 2021](#_bookmark74)). Therefore,

_T. dichotomus_ larvae and adult chitosan can be used as natural antimi-crobial agents.

- 1.  _Adsorption properties_

Selectively analyzing the adsorption effect of the adult chitosan, larvae chitosan, and commercial chitosan to on individual heavy metals and antibiotics, and after the chitosan stirred at 180 rpm for 24 h, it still shows flakes easy to remove. As can be seen from [Fig. 5](#_bookmark25) (a-b), there is a significant difference in the adsorption effect of different types of chi-tosan on heavy metals and antibiotics. The adsorption effect of the adult chitosan is stronger than larvae chitosan and commercial chitosan, with

the maximum adsorption capacity of Pb2+, Cu2+, Fe3+, SMZ, LEV and

TCH is 934, 462, 270, 67, 26, 22 mg/g, this may be due to the fact that Pb2+ and Cu2+ belong to the middle hard acid, while the amine group (—NH2) belongs to the middle hard base, and Fe3+ belongs to the hard

acid, so the reaction proceeds in a more stable direction. Further, under the acidic conditions created by HCl, some sulfur amide groups (-SO2NH-) in the SMZ molecule will be deprotonated into -SO2N—\-,

which forms electrostatic attraction with -NH + formed by the proton-

3

ation of the amine group ([Chen et al., 2013](#_bookmark39)). π-π conjugated structure

was formed between the ring-shaped structure of the chitosan and the benzene ring structure of SMZ ([Zhang et al., 2021](#_bookmark94); [Zhang, Wang, Jie,](#_bookmark90)

[Zhu, & Cheng, 2021](#_bookmark90)). However, the adsorption effect of chitosan with LEV and TCH was weak due to merely π-π conjugation and slight hydrogen bonding between chitosan and TCH ([Yao et al., 2020](#_bookmark89)). Due to the higher deacetylation degree of adult chitosan, the free amino group contained in the chitosan molecule is more, so it is conducive to the

adsorption. The Pb2+ adsorption performance of the adult chitosan product prepared in this study (934 mg/g) is better than that of most

reported modified chitosan (525 mg/g by chitosan/lignosulfonate ([Zhang, Wang, et al., 2021](#_bookmark90); [Zhang, Zhao, et al., 2021](#_bookmark94)), 204.89 mg/g by polyacrylic acid grafted magnetic chitosan nanocomposite ([Hu et al.,](#_bookmark51) [2020](#_bookmark51)), 196 mg/g by ninhydrin-functionalized chitosan ([Chen, Tang,](#_bookmark40) [et al., 2021](#_bookmark40); [Chen, Wei, et al., 2021](#_bookmark38))). Based on recent reports of simultaneous adsorption and removal of heavy metal ions and antibi-otics, due to the remarkable adsorption effect of adult chitosan on SMZ

and Pb2+, the adsorption behavior of heavy metals under single SMZ

condition and the adsorption behavior of antibiotics under single Pb2+ condition was studied ([Deng et al., 2020](#_bookmark42); [Jiang, Lin, & Mbog, 2018](#_bookmark54);

[Sekimoto, Nishihama, Yoshizuka, & Maeda, 2018](#_bookmark78)). As can be seen from [Fig. 5](#_bookmark25) (c-d), during the adsorption of heavy metals and antibiotics, the adsorption amount showed a trend of first increasing and then decreasing with the concentration of adsorbed substances changes, indicating that the two pollutants may have high and low concentration interference. Compared with single pollutants, the adsorption of adult

chitosan on SMZ and Pb2+ at moderate concentrations increased by 6%

and 5%, respectively. It may be due to the presence of a bridge between Pb2+ and chitosan in the acidic environment, while SMZ has electro-static interaction with chitosan ([Huang et al., 2017](#_bookmark52)). The two functions

show different effects with the change of concentration, which exhibits the change of overall adsorption effect of chitosan.

Based on the above studies, adsorption kinetics of adsorption SMZ and Pb2+ and composite contaminants were analyzed ([Fig. 6](#_bookmark26) and [Table 4](#_bookmark27)). For the adsorption of Pb2+, the equilibrium is reached within

100 min, and the adsorption of SMZ reaches the equilibrium within 200 min, both then remain stable until the test ends. In addition to the maximum adsorption amount, it may also be due to the chelating ability

of chitosan for Pb2+ is stronger than the electrostatic force of chitosan with SMZ, and shows the adsorption effect of Pb2+\-SMZ > Pb2+ > SMZ-Pb2+ > SMZ. Based on the correlation coefficient, it is considered that the adsorption of adult chitosan for SMZ and Pb2+ is more consistent

with the Pseudo 2nd kinetics. The adsorption isothermal line of adult chitosan is also analyzed. The Langmuir model is more suitable for describing the adsorption process of adult chitosan by comparing the correlation coefficient, and the maximum theoretical adsorption amounts of composite contaminants (Qe) is greater than the single heavy

metal or the single antibiotic, which may be because that Pb2+ prefer-

entially adsorbed on the chitosan surface promoted the adsorption of SMZ to chitosan. As shown in Table S2, the effect of adult chitosan on ΔGΘ of Pb2+ and SMZ at different temperatures indicated that the re-

action was spontaneous, and as the temperature increased, the ΔGΘ

decreased gradually, indicating that high temperature was conducive to the adsorption reaction. According to the analysis of the value of ΔHΘ factor, at 25–40 kJ⋅mol—1, there is both physical adsorption and chem-

ical adsorption, which is consistent with the study results of adsorption

isotherm ([Fan et al., 2017](#_bookmark45)). The used adult chitosan was filtered, and

The desorbed and re-generated materials were washed with distilled water to neutral, and the adsorption experiment after regeneration was carried out. It can be seen that the highest regeneration rate was achieved by using 0.1 mol/L HCl as eluent, both for single and compound pollutants (see Table S2 for the recovery ratios). The regeneration experiment was repeated to verify the

stability of adult chitosan (see Fig. S5 for the regeneration study). The results showed that the adsorption capacity is still 87% for Pb2+\-SMZ, 85% for SMZ- Pb2+, 82% for Pb2+ and 79% for SMZ after repeated three times.

After comprehensive comparison, the adult _T. dichotomus_ is more suitable for the preparation of chitosan, because its chitosan yield and degree of deacetylation are higher than that of the larvae, and adult chitosan has more excellent antimicrobial properties and contaminants adsorption abilities.

# Conclusions

In this study, chitosan with uniform mesh-like fiber structure was extracted from larvae and adults of _T. dichotomus_ by hydrothermal deacetylation, which was used for the adsorption of heavy metals-antibiotic composite contaminant. The degree of deacetylation, molec-ular weight, crystallinity, 13C NMR, FT-IR and TGA characterization of

_T. dichotomus_ as the source of chitosan and the effectiveness of the hy-drothermal deacetylation method were confirmed. The adsorption ca-

pacity of adult chitosan on Pb2+ and SMZ was in the order of Pb2+\-SMZ

\> Pb2+ > SMZ-Pb2+ > SMZ, and the adsorption capacity of adult chi-

tosan was higher than that of most reported modified commercial chi-tosan and adsorbing materials. The adsorption process is more consistent with pseudo-second kinetic equation and Langmuir model, and the adsorption process is spontaneous at room temperature, showing good regenerability. The adsorption performance and mecha-nism data show that the metal cations of hard acid and the sulfuramide group in SMZ molecules may be the main objects of chitosan adsorption, and in the composite system. These significant results indicate that

_T. dichotomus_ chitosan has great potential in metal-antibiotic composite adsorption as an alternative to commercial chitosan for the removal of complex contaminants from water.
